frase_gancho.texto: A rebozo that serves as a wrap, a cradle, and a jewel.

puente_narrativo.texto: From the rebozo, we move on to a painting of celebration. Look for a mural signed by Pablo O’Higgins, a painter born in the United States, whose title speaks of a Purépecha wedding.

guion_corto.texto: This Purépecha rebozo comes from the Paracho region, in Michoacán, and is woven on a backstrap loom. It is a long cloth, made of fine cotton or silk threads, that covers a woman from her head to her hips. The most admirable part is the ends: the fringes, called rapacejo, are knotted by hand, one by one, forming designs of arches and stars. Making a single rapacejo can take weeks. In the lives of Purépecha women, the rebozo is used to keep out the cold, to cover the head in church, to carry a child on the back, and to dress up for festivals. It is a useful, intimate, and elegant garment that accompanies a woman her whole life.

guion_largo.texto:
There is a garment that seems simple and hides a great deal: the rebozo. A long, thin cloth without any seams, which a woman drapes over her shoulders or head. With it she keeps warm in the mountains, shields herself from the sun, covers herself when entering a church, carries her child on her back, or carries her purchases from the market. And it also serves to adorn. Few garments do so much with so little cloth.

This rebozo was woven on a backstrap loom, the same kind you saw in the [textile collection](mna_s12_acervo_textil): a weaver, one end tied to her body and the other to a post, and the threads crossing with each pass of the shuttle. The thread is fine, made of cotton or silk, and is dyed with natural dyes, among them indigo, which gives the blue. That is why the shades have a depth that cannot be achieved with industrial colors.

Now look at the ends. Here is the most laborious part: the rapacejo. These are the leftover threads of the warp, knotted by hand one by one to form figures: arches, flowers, stars, sometimes names. There are those who spend weeks on a single rapacejo. It is said that a very fine rebozo can pass whole through a ring, and there are some that take months to weave. Sometimes that work is done by someone other than the weaver, a specialist in it known as the empuntadora. A garment can thus have two signatures. And the rebozo is worn in many ways: over the head, crossed over the chest, tied at the back to carry a child. Each way of wearing it tells something, from the cold of the day to the festival being celebrated.

Where does the rebozo come from? It is a matter of debate. Some think it blends Indigenous ideas, such as the use of long cloths for carrying, with influences from Spanish mantillas and from the shawls that arrived from Asia on the Manila galleon. However it came about, the rebozo ended up as one of the most recognizable garments of Mexico, and one of those most shared by Indigenous and mestizo peoples.

Its use goes beyond the practical. A woman may wear a rebozo from her youth, and sometimes her mother or grandmother gives it to her. It is used at baptisms, at weddings, and there are those who assure that it accompanies a person until their farewell. It is, for that reason, a garment full of affection, as well as a wrap.

Notice that the four pieces in this hall arise from materials of the region: the pine of the granary, the light wood of the mask, the copper of the workshop, and the cotton or silk of the loom. Each craft has its town, and each town has its specialty. Perhaps the most interesting thing about the Purépecha is this: over the centuries, they have preserved a strong identity through the work of their hands.

Before moving on, an invitation: look for a rebozo when you leave the museum. In the market, on a street, in a home. You are likely to see one, and now you will know how much there is in every thread.

texto: Look closely at the rapacejo: follow with your eyes one design in the knotted fringes
Find the blue of the indigo among the threads
Imagine how many uses it has: wrap, cradle, cloak, bag

texto.Region: Purépecha Plateau (Aranza, Paracho and Angahuan, Michoacán)
texto.Technique/Material: Cotton and wool spun and woven on a backstrap loom (patakua), hand-knotted fringe and indigo dyes
texto.Function: Everyday and ceremonial garment, shelter and maternity carrier

texto.pregunta: Myth: The rebozo is an unimportant garment, just a shawl for the cold.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It serves as a wrap, a cradle, a bag, and a formal garment, and it accompanies many women their whole lives. The hand-knotted fringes can take weeks.
